You are reverse-engineering a Python program's behavior as a BLACK BOX by running a precompiled executable.

Executable: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable
Source (Python, for reference):
    import argparse
    from furl import furl
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--d', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.fragment.__setattr__('str', args.b) or f.fragment)   # LINE1
    print(f.fragment.add(args.c))                                # LINE2
    print(f.fragment.set(args.d, 'value'))                       # LINE3
    print(f.url)                                                 # LINE4

RUN IT LIKE: /workspace/dataset/test12_executable --a "<A>" --b "<B>" --c "<C>" --d "<D>"
Never use the 'python' command. Do not read furl source; it is not available. Probe empirically.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (do not re-derive, but DO stress-test if in your area):
- --b is completely ignored: __setattr__('str', b) sets a dead instance attribute, no effect, returns None.
- LINE1 prints str(fragment) as parsed from A.
- LINE2 = fragment.path.add(C) then print str(fragment).
- LINE3 = fragment.path.load(D); fragment.query.load('value'); print str(fragment)  -> query is always literally 'value'.
- LINE4 prints the whole URL with the mutated fragment.
- Fragment str = path + '?' + query when both non-empty, else path+query. When query non-empty, literal '?' chars inside the fragment PATH are escaped to %3F; when query is empty they stay raw.
- furl DECODES percent-escapes on parse and RE-ENCODES on output: '%41%42' -> 'AB'; '%2F' inside a path segment -> stays '%2F'; lone '%' -> '%25'; 'a%zz' -> 'a%25zz'.
- Scheme and host are lowercased. Default ports dropped (http:80, https:443) but non-default kept (http:443 kept).
- URL query: '+' decodes to space, space encodes to '+'. 'a=b&c&d=' round-trips exactly (key-only 'c' vs empty-value 'd=' are distinct).

METHOD: run MANY probes (60+), vary one thing at a time, use printf %q or cat -A style to make whitespace visible, and note exit codes and stderr separately. Prefer a bash loop over a case list.

DELIVERABLE: a precise, implementable specification of YOUR assigned area: exact algorithm/rules, character sets (list the literal safe characters), ordering of operations, and a table of at least 25 concrete input->output examples you actually observed (verbatim). Call out anything surprising or that you could not determine. Be rigorous: an implementer will code directly from your spec with no access to the executable.


AREA: argparse command-line parsing behavior ONLY (not furl).
Determine exactly how the CLI parses process argv so it can be reimplemented by hand in Node:
- required args missing (one, several, all) -> exact stderr text, exit code, usage line wording, order of missing names.
- '--a=value' vs '--a value' forms. '--a' with no following token. Values that look like flags ('--a --b' , '--a -1', '--a=-x').
- Prefix/abbreviation matching: does '--' + partial work? There are options --a --b --c --d and -h/--help. Try '-a' (single dash), '--A' (case), unknown '--e'.
- Repeated options ('--a 1 --a 2') -> which wins.
- Empty string values, values with spaces/newlines/unicode, values starting with '-'.
- Extra positional arguments -> error text.
- '--help'/'-h' exact stdout text and exit code. Bare '--' separator handling.
- Interspersed ordering (--c before --a).
Report exact stderr strings verbatim including the program name shown in usage, and exit codes.

This happens even if required options are missing, even if unknown options appeared earlier, and even if extra tokens follow. Verified: `-h`, `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `-help`, `-hx`, `--help extra`, `-h --a`, `--nope --help`, `--a p --b y --c z --d w --help` all print help and exit 0.

HELP DOES NOT FIRE IF CONSUMED AS A VALUE POSITION: `--a -h ...` does NOT print help; it errors with 'argument --a: expected one argument' (because -h is option-like, --a finds no value). `--a=-h ...` passes the literal string '-h' as the value of --a and runs normally. Tokens after a bare `--` are never treated as options, so `-- -h` does not print help.

ERROR OUTPUT SHAPE: all parse errors write TWO lines to STDERR (stdout empty) and exit with code 2:
line1 = the usage line (same text/wrapping as in help)
line2 = `<prog>: error: <message>`
The error message line is NEVER wrapped, regardless of terminal width.

MISSING REQUIRED OPTIONS: message is `the following arguments are required: ` followed by the missing option strings joined with ', '. The order is the DECLARATION order --a, --b, --c, --d, NOT the command-line order. Only options never supplied are listed. Exit 2.

PRECEDENCE OF ERRORS (strict order): (1) help action -> exit 0; (2) 'expected one argument' / 'ambiguous option' / 'ignored explicit argument' errors, raised the moment the offending token is scanned (left-to-right); (3) 'the following arguments are required: ...'; (4) 'unrecognized arguments: ...'. So `-a x --a p --b y --c z --d w` yields 'unrecognized arguments: -a x' (nothing missing), while `-a x --b y --c z --d w` yields 'the following arguments are required: --a' (the required check runs before the leftover check).

VALUE ATTACHMENT FORMS: both `--a VALUE` (separate token) and `--a=VALUE` (single token, split at the FIRST '=') are accepted and equivalent. `--a=x=y` gives value 'x=y'. `--a==x` gives value '=x'. `--a=` gives the empty string. An empty separate token (`--a ''`) also gives the empty string.

WHEN THE NEXT TOKEN CAN BE A VALUE: for the separate-token form, the following token is consumed as the value UNLESS it 'looks like an option'. A token looks like an option iff: it is non-empty, its first character is '-', it is not exactly '-', it does not look like a negative number, and it contains no space character. Consequences that were verified: `--a -1` -> value '-1'; `--a -1.5` -> value '-1.5'; `--a -` -> value '-'; `--a '-x y'` -> value '-x y' (contains a space); `--a ' --b'` -> value ' --b' (contains a space); `--a -x` -> ERROR expected one argument; `--a -1abc` -> ERROR; `--a -1e5` -> ERROR (not a plain decimal number); `--a --` -> ERROR; `--a --b` -> ERROR; `--a --b=1` -> ERROR; `--a -h` -> ERROR. The negative-number exemption applies because no registered option looks like a negative number; the matcher accepts optional-sign integers and floats such as -1, -1.5, -0, -.5 but not -1e5.

MISSING VALUE ERROR TEXT: `<prog>: error: argument --a: expected one argument` (option string is the one the user typed, prefixed by 'argument '). For the help option it is rendered as `argument -h/--help: ...` (all option strings joined with '/').
REPEATED OPTIONS: last occurrence wins, silently (store action overwrite). `--a 1 --a 2` -> value '2'. `--a=x ... --a=q` -> value 'q'. Mixing forms is fine.
INTERSPERSED / ANY ORDER: options may appear in any order; `--d w --c z --b y --a p` behaves identically to `--a p --b y --c z --d w`.

LONG-OPTION ABBREVIATION IS ENABLED (allow_abbrev default True). A token beginning with '--' that is not an exact option name is matched against all long option names by PREFIX. Exactly one match -> that option; zero matches -> unrecognized argument; two or more matches -> ambiguous-option error. Since the long names are --help, --a, --b, --c, --d, the only useful abbreviations are --h, --he, --hel (all -> --help). '--a' etc. are already full names, so nothing shorter exists for them. Matching is CASE-SENSITIVE: --A, --B, --A=1 are unrecognized, never matched to --a/--b.

AMBIGUOUS OPTION: the only reachable ambiguity is the token `--` followed by '=' (e.g. `--=x`), which splits into prefix '--' and explicit arg 'x'; the empty prefix matches every long option. Message: `ambiguous option: --=x could match --help, --a, --b, --c, --d` — candidates are listed in registration order and only long ('--') option strings are listed. Exit 2.

NOT-A-PREFIX IS UNRECOGNIZED: `--ab x ...` and `--aa=1 ...` do not match --a (the typed string must be a prefix of the option name, not the other way round). `--ab x` therefore leaves --a unset and the required-check fires first: 'the following arguments are required: --a'.

SINGLE-DASH TOKENS: '-h' is the only registered short option. Any other single-dash token ('-a', '-x', '-ax', '-help'... except those that resolve via the rules below) is an unknown optional and lands in 'unrecognized arguments'. Note `-a x` produces unrecognized '-a x' — BOTH tokens, because the unknown optional consumes nothing and 'x' then becomes an unmatched positional.

SHORT-OPTION CLUSTERING WITH -h: `-hx` is parsed as -h followed by leftover '-x'; because -h is a help action it prints help and exits 0 before the leftover matters. `-help` likewise prints help (parsed as -h + '-elp' via the single-dash long-prefix path). BUT an explicit '=' is rejected: `-h=x` -> `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` (exit 2). Same for abbreviations with '=': `--he=x` and `--hel=1` -> `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'x'` / `'1'`. Rule: for a zero-argument option, an attached value written with '=' is an error; an attached value written without '=' is re-scanned as further single-dash options.

BARE '--' SEPARATOR: the first '--' terminates option parsing; every token after it is treated as a positional. Because the parser defines no positionals, '--' is NOT stripped and it plus everything after it end up in 'unrecognized arguments'. Verified: `--a p --b y --c z --d w --` -> 'unrecognized arguments: --'; `... -- extra` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- extra'; `... -- --` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- --'; `... -- -h` -> 'unrecognized arguments: -- -h' (help suppressed). Options appearing after '--' are not parsed, so `--a p --b y -- --c z --d w` errors with 'the following arguments are required: --c, --d'. Note: '--' written as a VALUE via '=' is fine: `--a=--` gives value '--'.

UNRECOGNIZED ARGUMENTS: message is `unrecognized arguments: ` followed by the leftover tokens joined by a single space, in original argv order, verbatim (no quoting/escaping). An empty-string leftover therefore renders as nothing, producing a trailing space after the colon: `unrecognized arguments: ` (observed for both `... ''` and `'' --a p ...`). A leftover containing spaces is printed raw, so the join is ambiguous/lossy (e.g. leftover ' --e' prints as 'unrecognized arguments:  --e' with two spaces).

EXTRA POSITIONALS: any bare token not consumed as a value is a leftover positional and reported by the 'unrecognized arguments' rule. `... zzz --e -1` -> 'unrecognized arguments: zzz --e -1'. A lone '-1'/'-1.5' after all options is also unrecognized (it is treated as a positional, not an option).

VALUE CONTENT IS PASSED THROUGH UNMODIFIED BY THE CLI: empty strings, spaces, tabs, newlines, non-ASCII/UTF-8 (e.g. 'héllo→'), leading '-', '#', '=', and '--' all reach the program byte-for-byte; any transformation observed in stdout is furl's doing, not argparse's.

NON-UTF-8 BYTES: argv is decoded with surrogateescape, so invalid byte sequences survive parsing but crash later. `--a $'\xff\xfe' --b y --c z --d w` exits 1 with a Python traceback on stderr ending in `UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode characters in position 0-1: surrogates not allowed` plus a PyInstaller line `[PYI-7972:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!`. Exit code 1 (not 2).

TERMINAL WIDTH: the usage line is wrapped by argparse using width = COLUMNS - 2 (COLUMNS from the environment; default 80 when unset, even when stdout is not a tty). The usage line is 53 chars, so it stays on one line for COLUMNS >= 55 and wraps for COLUMNS <= 54, with continuation lines indented to align under the prog name (25 spaces = len('usage: test12_executable ')). Option help entries in --help are wrapped/reflowed by the same width. For a faithful Node reimplementation, hardcode the 80-column (unwrapped) form unless COLUMNS is set.

EXIT CODES SUMMARY: 0 = successful parse (program then runs) or help displayed; 2 = any argparse error (missing required, expected one argument, unrecognized arguments, ambiguous option, ignored explicit argument); 1 = program-level exception after successful parse (e.g. surrogate bytes).
STREAMS: help goes to stdout only; all errors (usage line + error line) go to stderr only. Successful runs print exactly 4 lines to stdout and nothing to stderr.
input.safeCharacters: N/A — argparse performs no character encoding/escaping. Argument values are passed to the program byte-for-byte (decoded with UTF-8 + surrogateescape). The only characters with parsing significance are: leading '-' (marks a token as option-like), '=' (splits an option token into name and attached value at its first occurrence), the space character (its presence anywhere in a token makes the token NOT option-like), and the exact token '--' (end-of-options separator). Digits/'.'/'-' combining into a plain decimal number make an otherwise option-like token acceptable as a value.
